Science, nutrition, full-time training and better technique: each generation starts from a higher floor.

scenes.title: Sixty home runs isn't always sixty home runs
caps: Sixty home runs in 1927, when a team hit one about every three games, is a much bigger feat than seventy in 1998, when teams hit nearly three times as many.
And an athlete of the 1950s, with little weight training or sports science, can't be compared with a full-time professional of today without controlling for these changes.

First, the game itself changes. When every team scores more, each goal is worth a little less, like money in an inflated economy. So every other season is first converted to the scoring level of the season being judged.
NHL teams scored 3.97 goals a game in 1985–86 and 2.57 in 2003–04.
Home runs, points and yards get the same treatment.

caps: Then each performance is compared with only the best by everyone else in the 15 seasons before and after: each season's leader, the top one percent of their league.
They trained, ate and competed with much the same science and coaching, so together they set the standard for the best of that time: the elite curve.
The usual spread of the best around the elite curve is one standard deviation: about two-thirds of these elite seasons sit within one of it, and 95% within two.
Barry Bonds's 73 in 2001 is the record, but only 2.0 standard deviations above the elite curve: McGwire's 70 in 1998 is worth about 75 in 2001 terms. Not enough to crack this list.

cues: Athletes keep getting better. Since 1950, world records in athletics and swimming have improved by about twenty-three percent in the typical event.
Science, nutrition, full-time training and better technique: every generation starts from a higher floor.

The games themselves also change. Sixty home runs in 1927, when teams hit one every three games, is a much more impressive feat than hitting seventy in 1998, when teams were hitting nearly three times as many.
An athlete of the 1950s, with little weight training or nutrition science, can't be compared with today's full-time professionals without controlling for these changes.
So I looked for the biggest statistical outliers in team sports history in two steps. Step one: every other performance is converted to the scoring level of the season being judged.
For example, in hockey's run-and-gun 1980s, teams scored almost four goals a game. In 2003–2004, about two and a half.
Step two: each season is compared with only the best of everyone else in the fifteen seasons before and after. Each of these players was in the top one percent of their league that season.
They trained and competed with much the same science, so together they set the standard for the best of their time. Let's call that the elite curve.

The usual spread of the best around that curve is one standard deviation. The score we assign our athletes is how many standard deviations a performance sits above it. About two thirds of these elite seasons sit within one standard deviation of the elite curve, and ninety-five percent within two.

Barry Bonds's seventy-three home runs are the record, but only two standard deviations above the elite curve. Impressive for sure, but in his era, the other best hitters were that good. And two standard deviations doesn't crack the top of our list.
